title: Wine Tasting Hangover: Does Wine Tasting Get You Drunk?
excerpt: Does wine tasting get you drunk? The pour math behind a tasting flight, honest spitting etiquette, why red wine hits harder, and how to enjoy wine country without the hangover.
metaDescription: Does wine tasting get you drunk? How tasting pours add up, spitting etiquette, the tannin and sulfite question, and how to skip the wine tasting hangover.
author: DHM Guide Team
tags: does wine tasting get you drunk
content:
**The honest answer first:** yes, wine tasting can absolutely get you drunk, and it gives a lot of people a surprisingly rough hangover. The pours are small, so it doesn't *feel* like much drinking. But a typical tasting flight adds up to roughly one to three standard drinks, and many people visit two, three, or four wineries in an afternoon. That can quietly reach six to ten drinks over a few hours, often in the sun, on a light lunch, with very little water. Most people at a tasting don't spit, and the wines poured at many wineries are on the stronger side. Put that together and the next morning makes sense.

**The quick rules:** Count your pours, not your glasses. Eat a real meal before the first winery. Drink a glass of water at every stop. Use the dump bucket without guilt, and spit if you want to taste a lot of wines. Limit yourself to two or three wineries, and never drive yourself. Book a driver, a tour, or a sober friend.

> **This is not medical advice.** This article explains general research and guidance on alcohol for education only. It doesn't replace a doctor who knows your health history. **See a doctor if** wine reliably triggers migraines, you get hives, wheezing, chest tightness, or swelling of the lips or throat after drinking wine (these can be signs of an allergy or sulfite sensitivity, especially if you have asthma), you can't keep fluids down for most of a day after drinking, or you take medication that carries an alcohol warning. **Call 911** if someone is confused, can't stay awake, is vomiting while drowsy, has slow or irregular breathing, or has cold, clammy, pale or bluish skin. Those are signs of alcohol poisoning, and the person should not be left to "sleep it off."

## Does Wine Tasting Get You Drunk? The Pour Math

Most people underestimate a tasting because each pour looks like a sip. The way to see the real picture is to add it up using the idea of a **standard drink**.

In the US, one standard drink contains about 14 grams of pure alcohol. For wine at 12% alcohol by volume (ABV), that's a 5-ounce glass. If you want the full background, our guide to [what a standard drink is](/never-hungover/what-is-a-standard-drink) walks through the math for every type of drink.

Tasting pours vary by winery, but they usually fall somewhere between 1 and 2 ounces, and some places pour closer to 3. A flight is commonly four to six wines. Here's what that looks like:

| Tasting scenario | Total wine | Standard drinks at 12% ABV | Standard drinks at 14.5% ABV |
|---|---|---|---|
| 5 pours of 1 oz | 5 oz | about 1 | about 1.2 |
| 5 pours of 1.5 oz | 7.5 oz | about 1.5 | about 1.8 |
| 6 pours of 2 oz | 12 oz | about 2.4 | about 2.9 |
| 3 wineries, 5 pours of 1.5 oz each | 22.5 oz | about 4.5 | about 5.4 |
| 4 wineries, 6 pours of 2 oz each | 48 oz | about 9.6 | about 11.6 |

If you want to do the math yourself: multiply ounces of wine by the ABV, then divide by 0.6 (the ounces of pure alcohol in one US standard drink). Six 2-ounce pours of a 14.5% Zinfandel is 12 × 0.145 = 1.74 ounces of alcohol, divided by 0.6, which is about 2.9 standard drinks.

That last row in the table isn't an extreme day. It's four stops with generous pours. For reference, a full 750 ml bottle of 12% wine is about five standard drinks, so a big tasting day can mean drinking the equivalent of two bottles without ever ordering a glass. Our page on [how many drinks are in a bottle of wine](/never-hungover/how-many-drinks-in-a-bottle-of-wine) has the bottle-by-bottle breakdown.

### Why it creeps up on you

A few things about tastings make the total higher than people expect:

- **The ABV is often higher than you assume.** Many wines from warm regions, especially big reds like Zinfandel, Syrah, Cabernet Sauvignon, and Grenache, commonly land between 14% and 15.5%. A wine at 15% has 25% more alcohol than one at 12%.
- **The pours drift.** A friendly host tops you up, pours a "bonus" library or reserve wine, or offers a second taste of the one you liked. These rarely feel like extra drinks, but they are.
- **Fortified and dessert wines come last.** Port-style wines are often around 19% to 20% ABV. A small pour at the end of a flight carries more alcohol than its size suggests.
- **Sparkling wine comes first.** Many flights start with bubbles. There's some research suggesting carbonation can speed up how quickly alcohol is absorbed, though the effect varies from person to person. Either way, it's an early pour on an often empty stomach.
- **It's spread out, so it feels gentle.** Over a few hours, the buzz builds slowly. That makes it easy to lose track of how much you've had until you stand up from the last table.

### How fast your body clears it

Your liver clears alcohol at a fairly fixed pace, roughly one standard drink per hour for many adults, though this varies a lot with body size, sex, genetics, and other factors. Nothing you do speeds that up meaningfully. Coffee, cold showers, and food after the fact don't lower your blood alcohol faster. Our guide on [how long it takes to sober up](/never-hungover/how-long-does-it-take-to-sober-up) explains why.

So if you drank the equivalent of eight standard drinks across an afternoon of tasting, a good portion of that is still in your system at dinner, and some may still be there when you go to bed. That's why "I only had tastes" is not a safe way to judge whether you can drive.

## Spitting: The Etiquette and the Honest Truth

Professional wine judges and sommeliers often taste dozens of wines in a session. They manage it by **spitting**. Every tasting room has a spittoon or dump bucket for exactly this reason, and using it is normal, not rude.

### Is it rude to spit or dump at a tasting?

No. Staff at wineries see it all day, and many appreciate it because it means you're tasting seriously. A few tips to make it feel natural:

- **Dumping is the easy version.** If you've tasted a wine and don't want the rest of the pour, tip it into the dump bucket. Nobody keeps score of how much you finish.
- **Ask for a smaller pour.** You can simply say "just a splash, please" or "half pours for me." Most hosts are happy to do it.
- **Share a flight.** Many couples and friends split a single flight. You still taste everything, and you each drink half as much.
- **If you want to spit, do it neatly.** Take a small sip, move it around your mouth, then lean over the bucket and spit in a short, controlled stream. Some people bring their own small cup to spit into, which is less awkward at a crowded bar.
- **Skip the ones you already know you don't like.** You don't have to try every wine on the list.

### The honest part: most people don't spit

Spitting works, but let's be realistic. At a fun Saturday tasting with friends, most visitors swallow most of what they're poured. That's fine, as long as you count it. The pour math above assumes you're drinking what's poured, because that's what most people actually do.

Even when you do spit, it isn't a perfect zero. Some wine gets swallowed by accident, and a small amount of alcohol is absorbed through the lining of your mouth. Over a long tasting, that adds up to something, though it's far less than drinking. If you spit everything, you can taste a lot of wine and stay fairly clear-headed. If you spit "some of the time," expect to feel it.

A practical middle ground that many regular wine tasters use: spit or dump during the early part of the flight, and actually drink the one or two wines you love most.

## Why a Wine Tasting Hangover Feels So Bad

Plenty of people say a tasting day gives them a worse hangover than the same amount of beer or cocktails would. Some of that is real and some of it is circumstance. Here's what's likely going on.

### 1. It's usually more alcohol than you think

This is the main reason, and it's the least interesting one. Hangover severity tends to track how much alcohol you drank. A tasting day with three or four stops often adds up to more drinks than a normal night out, and that alone is enough to explain a rough morning.

### 2. Daytime drinking in the sun, with little water

Tastings often happen outdoors or on patios in warm wine country. Heat and sun make you sweat, and alcohol suppresses a hormone (vasopressin, also called antidiuretic hormone) that normally helps your kidneys hold on to water, so you pee more. Tasting rooms pour wine generously but water much less often. That combination leaves many people dehydrated by late afternoon. Dehydration isn't the whole cause of a hangover, but it adds to the headache, dry mouth, and fatigue. Our article on [whether alcohol dehydrates you](/never-hungover/does-alcohol-dehydrate-you) covers how much it actually matters.

### 3. Not enough food

A cheese plate and some crackers don't count as a meal. Food in your stomach slows how fast alcohol reaches your bloodstream, which helps keep your peak blood alcohol lower. Many tasting days start late morning after a light breakfast and push lunch back, which means your first two or three flights hit an emptier stomach.

### 4. Mixing lots of different wines (probably not the problem)

People often blame "mixing" for a bad tasting hangover. The evidence doesn't support that. A 2019 randomized trial published in the *American Journal of Clinical Nutrition* tested the old "beer before wine" rule and found that the order and combination of drinks didn't meaningfully change hangover severity. What mattered was how much people drank and how drunk they got. Tasting fifteen different wines isn't worse than drinking the same amount of one wine. It's just a very easy way to drink a lot.

### 5. Red wine compounds: congeners, tannins, histamine, and quercetin

This is where wine does differ from clearer drinks. Red wine contains more of the by-products of fermentation and aging, called **congeners**, than white wine or vodka. Research comparing darker and lighter drinks, such as bourbon versus vodka, has found that higher-congener drinks tend to produce somewhat worse hangovers at the same amount of alcohol. Our explainer on [congeners in alcohol](/never-hungover/congeners-in-alcohol) goes deeper.

Within that group, a few specific compounds get a lot of attention:

- **Tannins** are the compounds from grape skins, seeds, and stems (and from oak barrels) that make big reds feel dry and grippy in your mouth. Some researchers have suggested tannins may trigger headaches in some people, possibly through effects on serotonin. The evidence is limited and mostly comes from lab work and small studies, so there's no good evidence yet that tannins are a major hangover cause for most drinkers. Still, some people do notice they feel worse after very tannic reds.
- **Histamine** is found in higher amounts in red wine than white. People with lower activity of the enzyme that breaks down histamine may react with headaches, flushing, or a stuffy nose. Studies on wine histamine and headaches have been mixed. If this sounds like you, our page on [histamine intolerance and alcohol](/never-hungover/histamine-intolerance-and-alcohol) explains the signs.
- **Quercetin** is a natural compound in red grape skins. A 2023 lab study from the University of California, Davis proposed that the body converts quercetin into a form that can block one of the enzymes that clears acetaldehyde, a toxic by-product of alcohol. That could explain headaches that come on quickly after red wine in some people. It's an interesting idea, not a settled answer. Our [red wine headache guide](/never-hungover/red-wine-headache) covers this research in detail.

A long red-heavy tasting, especially at wineries known for bold, oaky, high-alcohol reds, stacks all of these at once.

### 6. Sulfites (less likely than you think)

Sulfites are the most common thing people blame, partly because US labels say "contains sulfites." The research doesn't point to them as a common headache or hangover cause. A few useful facts:

- Sulfites are added to most wines as a preservative, and some form naturally during fermentation.
- White and sweet wines often contain *more* sulfites than dry reds, yet many people get headaches mostly from reds.
- Many common foods, especially dried fruit, can contain more sulfites than wine.
- True sulfite sensitivity does exist, but it mostly shows up as breathing problems such as wheezing or tightness in the chest, particularly in people with asthma, rather than as a morning-after headache.

If you get wheezing or hives from wine, that's worth discussing with a doctor. If you get a headache and nothing else, sulfites are rarely the main culprit. Our guide to [sulfites in wine and headaches](/never-hungover/sulfites-in-wine-headaches) breaks down the evidence.

### 7. Sugar and late sweet wines

Sweet and dessert wines at the end of a flight add sugar along with higher alcohol. There's no strong evidence that sugar itself causes hangovers, but sweet wines are easy to sip and are often the strongest pours of the day. They also tend to come when you're already a few drinks in and judgment about "one more taste" is weakest.

### 8. Poor sleep

Even if you finish tasting at 5 p.m., many wine-country days roll into dinner and more wine. Alcohol helps you fall asleep but breaks up the second half of the night, which leaves you groggy and tired the next day. Poor sleep makes every other hangover symptom feel worse.

## How to Do a Wine Tasting Without the Hangover

The good news is that a few simple habits make a big difference. None of these require you to stop enjoying the day.

### Before you go

- **Eat a proper meal.** A breakfast or early lunch with protein, fat, and carbohydrates before your first stop helps slow alcohol absorption. Bring snacks for the car or tour bus.
- **Plan your stops.** Two or three wineries is a full day. Four or more is where most people go from "pleasant" to "regret." Space the stops out with a lunch in the middle.
- **Sort out transport first.** Book a driver, a tour, a rideshare, or choose a sober designated driver before you have a single sip. Deciding later, when you "feel fine," is where people get into trouble.
- **Hydrate in the morning.** Start the day with water rather than arriving already thirsty.

### At each winery

- **Drink a full glass of water at every stop.** Most tasting rooms have water on the bar or will happily pour you some. Ask for it at the start, not the end.
- **Use the dump bucket.** Taste, decide if you like it, and pour out what you don't want to finish.
- **Ask for half pours or share a flight.** This one change can cut your total alcohol in half.
- **Go slow.** You don't need to keep up with the host's pace. Let a few minutes pass between pours.
- **Eat the food.** If the winery offers a cheese or charcuterie plate, it's worth ordering, especially by the second stop.
- **Watch the reserve and dessert pours.** These are often the highest-alcohol wines of the day. It's fine to taste and dump them.

### Choose your wines strategically

If you know certain wines hit you harder, you can lean toward the ones that are easier on you:

- **Look for lower-ABV wines.** Many crisp whites, rosés, and lighter reds from cooler climates (think some Pinot Noir, Gamay, Riesling, Albariño, or Vinho Verde) run closer to 11% to 13%. The alcohol percentage is printed on the label or tasting sheet, so just ask.
- **If reds give you headaches,** try leaning toward whites and rosés, or lighter, less oaky reds. Our guide to [wines that don't give you a headache](/never-hungover/wines-that-dont-give-you-a-headache) has specific suggestions.
- **Don't rely on "sulfite-free" or "natural" labels** to prevent a hangover. The total alcohol you drink matters far more.

### After the tasting

- **Eat a real dinner.** Something with salt, protein, and carbohydrates helps settle your stomach and replace what you lost.
- **Keep drinking water, and consider electrolytes.** A drink with sodium and potassium can help if you sweated a lot in the heat. Our guide on [how to rehydrate after drinking](/never-hungover/how-to-rehydrate-after-drinking) covers what actually works.
- **Skip the "nightcap."** It's tempting to open a bottle you bought, but more wine on top of a tasting day is the most common reason the morning goes badly.
- **Be careful with painkillers.** Don't take acetaminophen (Tylenol) before bed to "head off" a headache, since it adds to your liver's workload while it's processing alcohol. If you take ibuprofen, take it with food, because alcohol already irritates the stomach. Check labels if you take any regular medication.

## Driving After Wine Tasting: Don't

This deserves its own section because it's the biggest real risk of a wine tasting day, much bigger than any hangover.

The legal blood alcohol limit for driving is 0.08% in most of the US (and 0.05% in Utah), and many countries set lower limits. Driving skills start to decline well before you reach the legal limit. Because tasting pours feel small and the day is spread out, many people genuinely believe they're fine to drive when they're not. You also can't reliably judge your own blood alcohol by how you feel, and you can't speed up how fast it drops.

Our guide on [what BAC is](/never-hungover/what-is-bac) explains how blood alcohol works and why the numbers vary so much from person to person.

The simple rule: **if you're tasting, you're not driving.** Wine regions are full of tour companies, drivers, and shuttles for exactly this reason. It's also worth knowing that wineries themselves have legal responsibilities around over-serving, and staff may stop pouring if a guest seems intoxicated. If that happens, it's a good sign to stop for the day.

## Does DHM Help With a Wine Tasting Hangover?

Many people heading out for a wine country weekend ask about hangover supplements. The most researched ingredient in this space is **DHM (dihydromyricetin)**, a compound from the Japanese raisin tree.

Here's the honest picture. DHM has been studied mostly in animals and in the lab, where it has shown effects on how the body handles alcohol and on liver health. Human data is much more limited, and there isn't strong clinical evidence yet that DHM prevents hangovers in people. It is not a way to drink more safely, it does not lower your blood alcohol, and it does not make it safe to drive.

Some people still like to take it as part of a sensible tasting plan, along with food, water, and pacing. If you want to try it:

- [Double Wood DHM](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B074N712FM?tag=dhmguide-20) is a budget-friendly, single-ingredient option at 1,000 mg per tablet.
- [No Days Wasted DHM Detox](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B0D4BWK6PH?tag=dhmguide-20) combines DHM with L-cysteine, milk thistle, and electrolytes.
- [Toniiq Ease](https://www.amazon.com/dp/B07S448GTT?tag=dhmguide-20) pairs a lower DHM dose with milk thistle and reishi.

Our [DHM dosage guide](/never-hungover/dhm-dosage-guide-2025) covers how much people take and when, and our [supplement reviews](/reviews) compare the main brands side by side. If you take prescription medication, check with your doctor or pharmacist before adding any supplement.

Supplements are the smallest lever here. Counting your pours, eating, drinking water, and limiting your stops will do far more.

## If You Already Have a Wine Tasting Hangover

If you're reading this the morning after, here's what helps most:

1. **Drink water steadily,** and add an electrolyte drink if you were out in the heat.
2. **Eat something gentle,** like toast, eggs, bananas, or broth. Even if you're not hungry, a little food helps settle your stomach and blood sugar.
3. **Rest.** Sleep is the one thing that reliably helps, because a hangover mostly resolves with time.
4. **Use a pain reliever carefully if you need one.** One standard dose with food, after the alcohol has cleared, following the label. Don't stack products, and talk to your doctor or pharmacist if you drink heavily most days or take other medication.
5. **Skip "hair of the dog."** More wine only postpones the hangover.

For more on the morning-after side of wine specifically, see our full [wine hangover guide](/never-hungover/wine-hangover-guide). Our broader guide on [how to prevent a hangover](/never-hungover/how-to-prevent-a-hangover) covers the habits with the best evidence for any kind of drinking.

Most hangovers ease within about 24 hours. If you're still vomiting and can't keep fluids down, feel confused, or have a severe headache that's unlike your usual ones, see a doctor.

## A Note on Wine Tasting and Your Drinking Overall

Wine tasting is meant to be about flavor, not volume. If you find that tasting days regularly turn into heavy drinking, or you're often waking up after them feeling unwell, it may help to set a firm limit before you go, such as "two wineries, shared flights, water at every stop." If cutting back feels harder than it should, talking to a doctor is a reasonable next step.

## The Bottom Line

- Wine tasting can get you drunk. A single flight is often one to three standard drinks, and a multi-winery day can easily add up to six to ten or more.
- High-ABV reds, generous pours, bonus tastes, and strong dessert wines push the total higher than people expect.
- Most hangovers from tasting come down to the amount of alcohol, plus sun, dehydration, too little food, and poor sleep.
- Red wine's congeners, histamine, tannins, and quercetin may make things worse for some people. Sulfites are less likely to be the problem than their reputation suggests.
- Spitting and dumping are normal and accepted. Half pours and shared flights are the easiest way to drink less without missing out.
- Never drive after a tasting. Book a driver or a tour before you start.

## Frequently Asked Questions

**Does wine tasting get you drunk?**

It can. Tasting pours are usually 1 to 2 ounces, and a flight of four to six wines often adds up to one to three standard drinks. Visit three or four wineries in an afternoon and you can reach six to ten standard drinks or more, which is enough to make most people drunk. Higher-alcohol reds and dessert wines push the total up further.

**How many tastings equal a glass of wine?**

A standard US glass of wine is 5 ounces. With 1-ounce pours, about five tastes equal one glass. With 2-ounce pours, it's about two and a half tastes. If the wines are stronger than 12% ABV, which many reds are, it takes fewer tastes to equal one standard drink.

**Is it rude to spit or pour out wine at a tasting?**

No. Spittoons and dump buckets are there for exactly that reason, and tasting room staff see it all day. You can also ask for a half pour or share a flight with a friend. None of these is considered rude.

**Does spitting wine stop you from getting drunk?**

Spitting removes most of the alcohol, so you can taste many wines and stay far more sober than if you swallowed them. It isn't completely zero, because some wine is swallowed accidentally and a little alcohol is absorbed in the mouth. If you spit some wines and drink others, count the ones you drink.

**Why do I get such a bad hangover from wine tasting?**

Usually because it was more alcohol than you realized, often drunk in the sun with little water and not enough food. Red wine also contains more congeners than clear drinks, plus compounds like histamine, tannins, and quercetin that may contribute to headaches in some people. Mixing different wines isn't the issue, since research suggests the total amount of alcohol matters much more than the variety.

**Are sulfites the reason wine tasting gives me a headache?**

Probably not for most people. White wines and dried fruit often have more sulfites than red wine, yet red wine is the more common headache trigger. True sulfite sensitivity usually causes breathing symptoms like wheezing, especially in people with asthma. If you have those symptoms, talk to a doctor.

**Can I drive after a wine tasting?**

It's safest not to. Tasting pours add up quickly, your liver clears only roughly one standard drink per hour, and you can't reliably judge your blood alcohol by how you feel. Book a driver, a tour, a rideshare, or choose a sober designated driver before you start.

**Does DHM prevent a wine tasting hangover?**

There's no strong clinical evidence that DHM prevents hangovers in people. Most of its research comes from animal and lab studies. It doesn't lower your blood alcohol or make it safe to drive. Some people take it alongside food, water, and pacing, but those habits matter far more than any supplement.
